slides.say: Given: x is equal to three, times five squared, times ten squared. Which of the following numbers does not divide x?

So x is already broken into pieces, and they ask which number does not divide it. Divide is the same as factor, so they're asking which choice is not a factor of x, which one you can't build out of x. And careful, one of the pieces, ten, isn't a prime. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, breaking everything into primes, and then dividing the real number.

[short pause] Remember the check from the lesson. A number divides x only if every prime it needs is in x, at least as many times. So first, every piece of x has to be a prime. Three is a prime, and five is a prime, but ten isn't.

So how do I unpack ten squared? Ten squared is ten times ten. And each ten is two times five. So ten squared is two times five, times two times five. That's two twos and two fives, two squared times five squared.
at: Ten squared is ten times ten

slides.say: Now careful here. A lot of students look at x, don't see a two anywhere, and cross out every even choice. But the twos are hiding inside the tens.

We're making a complete inventory of the prime factors in x. Count the copies from every part of the original product. So let's count. Five squared from the start, and five squared from the ten squared, that's four fives. Two twos, and one three. So x is two squared, times three, times five to the power of four.
at: times five to the power of four

slides.say: Now we'll break each answer choice into primes and compare what it needs with what x contains. Now the choices. Twenty is two times ten, and ten is two times five. So twenty is two squared times five. Two twos, and x has two. One five, and x has four. Everything is in stock, so twenty divides x, and choice number one is out.
Twenty-two is two times eleven. The two is there. But is there an eleven anywhere in x? No. Eleven is a prime that x simply doesn't have, so twenty-two can't divide x.

Can I circle it already? In the exam, yes, a missing prime settles it. Here, let's check the other two as well. Seventy-five is three times twenty-five, so three times five squared. One three and two fives, both in stock. Choice number three is out.

Sixty is six times ten, so two times three, times two times five. That's two squared, times three, times five. Two twos, one three and one five, all in stock. Out too. So twenty-two, choice number two is our answer.
at: choice number two is our answer

slides.say: So whenever a piece isn't a prime, like ten or six, unpack it into primes first.

[pause] Our second method, working out x as a number, and simply dividing. Five squared is twenty-five, and ten squared is a hundred. Three times twenty-five is seventy-five, and seventy-five times a hundred is seven thousand five hundred.
Twenty. Seven thousand five hundred over twenty is the same as seven hundred fifty over two, and that's three hundred seventy-five. A whole number, so twenty divides x, and choice number one is out.

Dividing by twenty-two means dividing by both its factors, two and eleven. Let's check whether both divisions can finish without a remainder. Twenty-two. Half of seven thousand five hundred is three thousand seven hundred fifty, and now I divide by eleven. Eleven times three hundred is three thousand three hundred, and eleven times forty is four hundred forty. Together, eleven times three hundred forty is three thousand seven hundred forty, and that leaves ten. A remainder, so twenty-two doesn't divide x.
at: is three thousand seven hundred forty

slides.say: Seventy-five. Seventy-five times a hundred is seven thousand five hundred, so it divides exactly. Out. Sixty. Seven thousand five hundred over sixty is seven hundred fifty over six, and that's a hundred twenty-five. Out too. So again, choice number two. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
